title: I'm building an AI tool to help traders find their edge
author: Icecoldobsidian
selftext:
Every trader has his trading strategy and believes that he knows what works and what does not. But how much does the trader actually know about his strategy based on his own trading data?

I am creating a Chartix trading journal to help you objectively analyze your trading and find out what exactly works and does not work for you.

Chartix will help you avoid tracking and analyzing your trades on your own by providing you with different trading performance statistics depending on the instrument, direction of the trade, weekdays, and so on,

find profitable setups and patterns for you, help you find the reasons for your losses and analyze which trades and patterns are the most losing 

Chartix can also help you collect charts and track your trades by allowing you to turn your chart images into journal entries and, finally, analyze the last trades using artificial intelligence to find profitable patterns.

Chartix, is still being developed and I would love to hear some feedback regarding this idea.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the split by setup is where a journal earns its keep. the catch is sample size, most people log maybe 20 trades per setup in a quarter, and at 20 a good setup and a bad one look about the same.

replies.author: Icecoldobsidian
replies.body: That’s right, and I think that’s where confidence intervals and awareness of sample size could make the analysis much more useful. In addition to simply ranking setups by profitability, the tool could also show its confidence level in those results and flag setups for which there is not enough data to draw meaningful conclusions yet.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the flag matters more than the interval. people skim past a confidence band, but "not enough trades yet" in red changes what they do. Quantradin does this, I built it (free, paper only), and the verdict it gives most often is "can't call it yet".

replies.author: Icecoldobsidian
replies.body: Valid point, but I would go even further and claim that accurate fills and running strategies based on actual prices is only half the story. Even with perfectly executed trades, a strategy may be found to be profitable just by pure luck, over-fitting, or performance in a certain market regime. How is Quantradin able to differentiate a true robust strategy from an accidental profitable one? This is where things get really interesting.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: it can't, fully. what it does: grades walk-forward with in-sample and out-of-sample shown side by side, and when there are too few trades the verdict says it can't call it yet instead of guessing. regime luck is the part I haven't solved. a rule that only ever saw one kind of market can still pass.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body:
I’d keep screenshot-derived journal fields provisional until they match an execution record: timestamps, partial fills, fees and position direction are easy to misread. For prop users, also tag the risk state at entry, so “bad signal” and “good setup taken outside the account’s risk budget” do not get merged into one AI conclusion.



We’re QATS. If you want to try a separate perpetuals-prop import, our Trading API exposes executions, orders, positions and account/risk state: [https://quantityproject.github.io/qats-trader-api/](https://quantityproject.github.io/qats-trader-api/) . It would need a dedicated adapter and pagination; history is capped rather than a guaranteed gap-free full-history export. Evaluations and initial funded accounts are simulated.
